summary.text: An integral domain is a nonzero commutative ring in which the product of any two nonzero elements is nonzero.
In one, if a ≠ 0, then ab = ac implies b = c, so a nonzero factor can be cancelled.
Integral domains generalize the ring of integers and give a setting that is useful for studying divisibility.

facts.label: Same idea, other words
facts.value: A nonzero commutative ring with no nonzero zero divisors

facts.label: Lives inside a field
facts.value: Every integral domain is a subring of some field

facts.label: Polynomial example
facts.value: The ring ℤ[x] of polynomials with integer coefficients is one

facts.label: Another name
facts.value: Some sources, notably Lang, call it an entire ring

items.prompt: In a ring of pairs multiplied entry by entry, (1, 0)⋅(0, 1) = (0, 0). Both factors are nonzero. What does this show about the ring?

options.label: It is an integral domain, since the pairs commute
It is a field, since both entries are invertible
It is an integral domain, since the product is zero
It is not an integral domain, since nonzero factors gave zero

items.explain: In an integral domain the product of two nonzero elements is nonzero. A product of two nonzero commutative rings breaks this, as the pair example shows.

items.prompt: In an integral domain you know that a ≠ 0 and that ab = ac. What can you conclude?

options.label: b = c
a is 1
b and c are both zero
Nothing, since cancelling is never allowed

items.explain: Every nonzero element of an integral domain has the cancellation property: ab = ac forces b = c.

items.prompt: Two nonzero matrices M and N are chosen so that everything N produces is sent to zero by M. What is the product MN, and what does it say about rings of n × n matrices with n ≥ 2?

options.label: MN is nonzero, so matrix rings are integral domains
MN is zero, so nonzero elements can multiply to zero
MN is nonzero, so matrix rings are fields
MN is zero, so M and N must both be zero

items.explain: When the image of N sits inside the kernel of M, MN = 0, so such matrix rings have nonzero elements whose product is zero and are not integral domains.

items.prompt: You build polynomials whose coefficients come from an integral domain. What can you say about the ring of those polynomials?

options.label: It is an integral domain too
It is never commutative
It is an integral domain only for one variable
It is always a field

items.explain: Rings of polynomials are integral domains if the coefficients come from an integral domain; this covers integer coefficients and complex coefficients in several variables.

items.prompt: You are handed an integral domain and want to place it inside a larger, friendlier structure. What can always hold a copy of it?

options.label: A matrix ring
A zero ring
A field
A ring with zero divisors

items.explain: An integral domain is a ring isomorphic to a subring of a field, and it can be embedded in its field of fractions.

items.prompt: A writer studies a ring where multiplication is not commutative, yet two nonzero elements never multiply to zero. Under the usual convention, what name fits?

options.label: An integral domain
An entire field
A zero ring
A domain

items.explain: The term integral domain is reserved for the commutative case, while domain covers the general case including noncommutative rings.
